request: how does a bill become a law in the United States?

composition.story: Follow a federal bill introduced in the House through committee review and votes in both chambers. Use Next to see when approval becomes law. This example keeps the text unchanged and ends with presidential signature. A veto instead requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber to override.

aha.observation: On this route, the bill becomes law after both chambers approve identical text and the President signs it.

parts.presentation: Use the approved card shell, with story and instructions above the experiment. Show ordered steps with wrapped labels and the active step. Keep progress here. Brief parameter-control budget: zero; navigation comprises Previous, Next, and Reset.

Arrange named regions in a fixed left-to-right path using the tested part's layout. Highlight only the active region; mute inactive regions. Preserve readable labels at native width. No motion or fabricated time.
Anchor beside the active region without covering labels. Identify its action and significance; leave numerical evidence in readouts.

Place compact readouts below the picture, with Status last as a persistent status line. Matching approvals count House and Senate passage of unchanged text. Counts use exact integers, with no rounding. The fixed reference is both chambers.

controls.label: Bill stage
controls.presentation: Use Previous and Next, retaining names when disabled at boundaries. Default to the first state; advance one integer index within the supplied states. Every state persists until learner action, including law. Provide accessible button names, visible focus, and keyboard activation. Reference captures show law.

controls.label: Reset
controls.presentation: Restore the first state and all defaults. Provide an accessible name, visible focus, and keyboard activation.

variants.label: House-origin bill, unchanged text, presidential signature

states.label: Introduced
states.sentence: A House member introduces the bill, which is referred to a House committee.
states.why: Introduction begins consideration; it does not enact the proposal.

states.label: House review
states.sentence: The House committee reviews the bill and reports it for House consideration.
states.why: In this example, the committee recommends advancing the bill without changing its text.

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: House committee reported bill; not law

states.label: House vote
states.sentence: The House debates and passes the bill, then sends it to the Senate.
states.why: House passage alone is insufficient; the Senate must also approve identical text.

states.label: Senate review
states.sentence: A Senate committee reviews the House-passed bill and reports it for Senate consideration.
states.why: This example follows committee review in both chambers; neither committee substitutes for a chamber's passage vote.

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Senate committee reported bill; not law

states.label: Senate vote
states.sentence: The Senate passes exactly the text that the House passed.
states.why: If the Senate changed the text, both chambers would need to approve an identical final version.

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Congress passed identical text; not yet law

states.label: President
states.sentence: The bill approved by both chambers is presented to the President.
states.why: Congressional passage and presidential signature are distinct actions on this route.

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Presented to President; not yet law

states.label: Law
states.sentence: The President signs the bill, making it federal law.
states.why: Both chambers approved identical text, and the President completed this route by signing.
